title: General Appropriations Act
summary: Texas Senate Bill 1 is the General Appropriations Act for the state fiscal biennium beginning September 1, 2025. It sets state appropriations and related conditions for state agencies, public education, health and human services, and other publicly funded programs. The Texas Legislature's official history records that the bill was signed by the Governor on June 22, 2025 and became effective September 1, 2025.
affects: State agencies, public education, health and human services, local governments, and recipients of state funding
changes: Establishes Texas state-budget appropriations and conditions for the 2025–2027 biennium
business_impact: Organizations that depend on state funding, contracts, grants, or agency programs should monitor the enacted appropriations and each agency's implementation decisions
suggested_action: Review the enacted bill and the Legislative Budget Board's budget materials for the programs relevant to your organization, then track agency implementation and contract or grant notices. This summary is a starting point and is not a substitute for the enacted text, agency guidance, or legal advice.

title: Voter-approval tax rate reduction
summary: SB 10 lowers the amount by which larger Texas cities and counties can increase property tax revenue year-over-year without triggering a mandatory voter election. Specifically, it cuts the automatic maintenance-and-operations growth cap from 3.5% to 2.5% for jurisdictions with populations over 75,000. The bill is the successor to SB 9 from the first special session, which passed the Senate but died before the House could act. SB 10 narrowed the applicable population threshold from 30,000 to 75,000, focusing the impact on larger cities and counties. The Comptroller's office has estimated the policy could cut hundreds of millions of dollars in cumulative local tax levies over the coming years.
affects: Cities and counties over 75,000 population
changes: Lowers the automatic property tax growth cap from 3.5% to 2.5% before voter approval is required
business_impact: May slow local property tax growth, affecting local government revenue and services
suggested_action: Municipal finance officers and bond advisors in affected cities and counties should model out revised revenue projections under the 2.5% cap and identify whether upcoming budgets will require voter-approval elections sooner than previously planned. Firms that advise local governments on budgeting, bond issuance, or tax rate elections should proactively reach out to affected clients to help them plan election timing and messaging, since more jurisdictions will likely need to go to voters for rate increases that previously didn't require one.

title: Texas Women's Privacy Act
summary: SB 8, the Texas Women's Privacy Act, requires restrooms, locker rooms, and sleeping quarters in government buildings, public schools, and state-funded facilities to be designated and used according to biological sex. The bill applies broadly across state agencies, public universities, correctional facilities, and domestic violence shelters. It establishes a civil penalty structure of at least $25,000 per violation for noncompliant facilities. Critically, it also creates a private civil right of action, meaning individuals can sue directly rather than relying solely on Attorney General enforcement. This significantly raises litigation exposure for covered institutions compared to typical state regulatory schemes.
affects: State agencies, public schools and universities, prisons, jails, and domestic violence shelters
changes: Requires restrooms/locker rooms designated by biological sex; sets civil penalties for violations
business_impact: Public institutions must update facility policies or face $25,000+ fines and lawsuits
suggested_action: Facility managers at public schools, universities, and state agencies should review and update restroom and locker room signage and access policies to align with the bill's definitions, and should consult legal counsel given the private right of action, since this is not just an AG enforcement risk. Institutions should also train front-line staff, including dorm supervisors, corrections officers, and shelter staff, on the new designation rules and document compliance decisions in writing, since private lawsuits will likely turn on whether an institution can show a good-faith compliance process.

title: Disaster preparedness and emergency manager licensing
summary: SB 2 is a broad disaster-preparedness overhaul that would create a tiered licensing system for emergency managers statewide. It also establishes a volunteer database for disaster response and touches related areas including aeronautics, meteorological data monitoring, and small-business disaster loans. The bill moved through significant legislative activity, including conference committee negotiations between the House and Senate. However, reporting indicates the bill ultimately stalled and did not receive final Senate approval, which conflicts with metadata showing conference committee action. This discrepancy should be verified directly against capitol.texas.gov before treating the bill as enacted law.
affects: Emergency managers, TDEM, local governments, volunteers
changes: Creates tiered emergency manager license, volunteer database, and disaster loan program
business_impact: Emergency management professionals need new licenses; note: bill stalled and missed final passage
suggested_action: Given the uncertain final status of this bill, emergency management consultants and disaster-response contractors should hold off on major compliance spending until the bill's status is confirmed directly at capitol.texas.gov. If it did pass, professionals currently working as emergency managers for municipalities should identify which license tier they'd fall into and begin the application process early, since a new licensing regime typically creates a backlog in its first year. Firms bidding on state disaster-response contracts should also monitor whether the new volunteer database becomes a required registration point for eligibility.

title: Real property theft and fraud offenses
summary: SB 16 creates new felony criminal offenses specifically targeting real property theft and title or deed fraud, a growing problem involving fraudulent deed filings used to steal home ownership. The bill sets a statute of limitations for prosecuting these new offenses and establishes procedures for victim restitution. It also introduces new photo ID verification requirements for filing certain property documents with county clerks. This adds a compliance step to real estate closing and recording workflows that did not previously exist. Over time, the ID requirement is intended to reduce fraudulent filings even as it adds friction to legitimate transactions.
affects: Property owners, title insurance companies, county clerks, and real estate closing attorneys
changes: Creates new felony crimes for deed/title fraud; requires photo ID to file property documents
business_impact: Title companies and clerks gain new ID-check duties; victims get restitution rights
suggested_action: Title companies and county clerk offices should update their document intake procedures now to require and log photo ID for anyone filing a deed, lien release, or related property document, and should train closing staff on the new ID-verification workflow before the effective date. Title insurers should also review underwriting guidelines, since the new restitution framework may affect how claims tied to fraudulent deed filings are handled and potentially reduce loss exposure once fraud drops. Real estate attorneys should update client-facing closing checklists to explain the new ID requirement so it doesn't cause last-minute closing delays.

title: Supplemental disaster relief appropriations
summary: SB 5 appropriates roughly $294 million from Texas's Rainy Day Fund largely in response to the 2025 Hill Country floods. The funding covers FEMA cost-share matching requirements, new flood warning siren installations, expanded meteorological forecasting infrastructure, and emergency responder training. The Governor's office is given adjustment authority to reallocate funds across these categories as needs shift over time. Unlike most bills in this set, SB 5 is purely a funding measure rather than a new regulatory mandate. It creates state grant and contracting opportunities rather than compliance obligations for private industry.
affects: Emergency management agencies, flood-affected counties, first responders, and disaster-response vendors
changes: Appropriates $294M in Rainy Day Fund money for FEMA match, flood sirens, forecasting, and training
business_impact: Disaster-response contractors and local governments gain access to new grant funding
suggested_action: Companies that sell flood siren systems, weather monitoring equipment, or emergency responder training should monitor TDEM and county procurement postings closely over the next 12 to 18 months, since this appropriation will flow through state and local government contracts. Firms should also build relationships with the counties named in the state's disaster declarations, as those counties will likely be first in line for grant-funded projects. Businesses should be prepared for a competitive bidding environment given the scale of funding suddenly available.

title: Outdoor warning sirens in flood-prone areas
summary: SB 3 requires the installation of outdoor warning siren systems in designated high-risk flash-flood zones across roughly 30 Texas counties under flood disaster declarations. The bill creates a state grant program administered through the Texas Water Development Board to help fund installation and ongoing maintenance. It is directly responsive to the Hill Country flood, where the absence of adequate early-warning systems was cited as contributing to loss of life. Local governments in affected counties will bear responsibility for procuring, installing, and maintaining the systems. The grant funding is designed to offset what would otherwise be a significant unfunded mandate on smaller counties.
affects: Roughly 30 counties under flood disaster declarations, municipalities, and the Texas Water Development Board
changes: Requires siren installation in high-risk flood zones and creates a state grant program to fund it
business_impact: Siren/alert-system vendors and local governments face new install and maintenance mandates
suggested_action: Siren and alert-system vendors should identify which of the roughly 30 named counties haven't yet installed adequate systems and proactively pitch installation and ongoing maintenance contracts, positioning around the new TWDB grant funding to make the case financially easier for county officials. Companies should also build a maintenance and service offering, not just installation, since the bill implies ongoing upkeep obligations for the counties — a recurring revenue opportunity beyond the initial build-out.

title: Groundwater permits and modeled available groundwater
summary: SB 58 would have required groundwater conservation districts to factor in 'modeled available groundwater,' a state-produced estimate of sustainable pumping levels, when deciding whether to issue large-volume water permits. This would have given districts a stronger scientific basis to deny or limit permits for high-volume groundwater withdrawals. The bill was filed at the start of the session but never advanced past introduction, meaning it received no committee hearings or floor votes. It ultimately did not pass this legislative session. Because similar proposals have surfaced in prior sessions, the underlying policy concept is likely to resurface.
affects: Groundwater conservation districts and companies holding or seeking large-volume groundwater permits
changes: Would require districts to weigh modeled available groundwater when issuing permits (bill filed, not passed)
business_impact: Companies seeking large groundwater transfer permits could face new limits if enacted
suggested_action: Since this bill did not pass, no immediate action is required, but companies with significant groundwater dependency in Texas, particularly data center operators and oil and gas companies using groundwater for hydraulic fracturing, should track whether this concept resurfaces in the next regular session. Proactively engaging with local groundwater conservation districts now, before a stricter standard becomes law, can help establish a track record that supports future permit renewals.

title: Handgun license eligibility for federal judges
summary: HB 161 would have expanded the definition of 'federal judge' for purposes of expedited handgun license issuance in Texas to specifically include U.S. immigration court judges. Immigration judges are administrative rather than Article III judges, and were previously excluded from this expedited eligibility category under existing law. The bill was filed early in the session but did not advance beyond that initial filing stage. It received no further legislative action and did not pass. The change, had it passed, would have affected only a narrow group of individual license applicants rather than any broader policy area.
affects: Federal immigration court judges
changes: Adds U.S. immigration court judges to the definition of 'federal judge' eligible for expedited handgun licenses (bill filed, not passed)
business_impact: No meaningful business impact — this is a narrow eligibility change affecting individual license applications, not a commercial or industry regulation.
suggested_action: No business action needed. This is relevant only to individual immigration court judges seeking Texas handgun licenses, and since it did not pass, there's nothing to act on unless it's refiled in a future session.

It contains no statutory language and creates no legal obligations of any kind. The resolution was filed and processed as a standard honorary measure with no further legislative action needed beyond adoption. It has no bearing on any industry, business, or regulatory framework.

business_impact: N/A — no business impact
suggested_action: No action needed.

title: Local emergency warning system opt-in via DMV
summary: HB 200 would have created a voluntary local emergency warning system tied to the driver's license application and renewal process. Residents applying for or renewing a license could opt in to share their contact information, including phone number, address, and email, with their local municipality or county for emergency alerts. An opt-out mechanism via written or text request was included to let residents withdraw at any time. The bill was filed but did not pass this session, continuing a pattern: nearly identical language has been filed repeatedly in prior sessions dating back to at least 2019 without success. If it does eventually pass, it would give local governments a state-facilitated contact database rather than requiring them to build one independently.
affects: Municipalities, counties, the Texas DMV, and driver's license applicants
changes: Lets residents opt in via driver's license application to share contact info with local emergency alert systems (bill filed, not passed this session)
business_impact: Minimal direct business impact; local governments could gain a new resident contact database
suggested_action: Companies selling emergency notification or reverse-911 alert platforms to municipalities should monitor this bill if refiled in future sessions, since a state-run, DMV-fed contact database could reduce municipalities' reliance on third-party-purchased contact lists. Vendors may want to consider positioning their platforms as complementary delivery and dispatch layers on top of any future state-provided contact database, rather than as competitors to it.

title: County authority to regulate impervious cover
summary: HB 188 would have explicitly granted Texas county commissioners courts the authority to regulate impervious cover, meaning pavement, rooftops, concrete, and other surfaces that prevent water absorption, in unincorporated areas. The stated purposes were reducing flood risk, promoting drainage, and encouraging nature-based flood mitigation features. This would represent a meaningful expansion of county authority, since Texas counties currently have very limited land-use and zoning power compared to cities. The bill has now been filed in multiple consecutive legislative sessions under nearly identical language, appearing previously as HB 117 and HB 2956, without ever passing. It did not pass this session either, though repeated flood events statewide continue to build pressure for eventual passage.
affects: County governments, land developers, and property owners in unincorporated areas
changes: Would let counties regulate impervious cover (pavement, roofs) to reduce flood risk (bill filed, not passed)
business_impact: Developers could face new county-level site coverage limits in unincorporated areas
suggested_action: Developers active in unincorporated Texas counties, particularly in fast-growing areas like Travis, Hays, Williamson, and Montgomery counties, should track this bill closely if refiled next session, since it has now been introduced in several consecutive sessions and public pressure from repeated flood events increases the odds of eventual passage. Developers should proactively model projects against likely impervious cover caps, since many Texas cities already use 15% residential and 45% commercial as reference points, so that site plans already in the pipeline aren't caught flat-footed if county authority is granted. Industry associations may also want to engage in the interim to help shape the specific cap percentages before the next filing.

title: Voter-approval tax rate reduction (1st special session)
summary: SB 9 was the first-special-session predecessor to SB 10, and would have lowered the automatic property tax revenue growth cap from 3.5% to 2.5% for taxing units with populations above 30,000. It passed the Senate on a strong 19-2 vote but died without House action before the special session concluded. The Comptroller estimated the bill would have cut cumulative local property tax levies by roughly $209 million in 2026, rising to $425 million by 2027. The underlying policy concept was revived in the second special session as SB 10, though with the population threshold raised to 75,000, narrowing its scope. The two-session persistence signals the legislature's strong intent to eventually enact some version of this cap regardless of the specific threshold.
affects: Cities and counties above 30,000 population
changes: Lowers automatic property tax growth cap from 3.5% to 2.5% before voter approval required; passed Senate, died before House action
business_impact: Would have constrained local government tax revenue growth; superseded by SB 10 in 2nd special session
suggested_action: This bill is dead — SB 10 is now the operative version. Municipal finance professionals should use SB 9's history mainly as context: it shows the state legislature is persistent on this policy, having advanced it twice in one year with only the population threshold changing. Bond advisors should assume this trend continues and build tax-rate-cap sensitivity into multi-year revenue projections for any Texas municipal client, even those currently below the 75,000-population threshold in SB 10, since the threshold has already moved once and could move again.
